non_conformance_description: Fine surface crack network observed on hot-rolled coil HR-1187, Line 1, concentrated in the mid-width region. Approximately 3% of coils in the shift showed the pattern under inspection light.
five_why: Why 1: Surface cracking appears after finishing rolling -> the strip experienced excessive thermal cycling before the final pass.
Why 2: Excessive thermal cycling occurred -> the reheat furnace zone-3 temperature overshot setpoint by ~40C during the shift.
Why 3: Zone-3 overshot -> the furnace's temperature control loop was running on a manual override left from a prior maintenance test.
Why 4: Manual override was left active -> the maintenance technician did not log the override or return the controller to auto mode at end of test.
Why 5 (root cause): the maintenance work instruction for furnace controller testing does not require a mandatory return-to-auto verification step before sign-off.
root_cause: The furnace maintenance test procedure has no mandatory step requiring verification that temperature control is returned to automatic mode before the furnace is released back to production.
corrective_action: Return zone-3 controller to automatic mode immediately; re-inspect all coils processed during the override window for crazing before release.
preventive_action: Add a mandatory 'return-to-auto' checklist item with technician and shift-supervisor dual sign-off to the furnace maintenance test work instruction; interlock the furnace HMI to alarm if manual override remains active beyond 30 minutes.
effectiveness_verification: Zero furnace override-related crazing incidents over the next 20 production days; maintenance work-order audit confirms 100% dual sign-off compliance for furnace tests in the same period.

non_conformance_description: Operator on Line 3 night shift flagged crazing on the trailing end of coil HR-1340, roughly 1.5m of affected length, first noticed on the 6th coil of a new steel grade changeover.
five_why: Why 1: Crazing appeared only on the trailing end -> that section cooled at a faster rate than the rest of the coil.
Why 2: Faster cooling on the trailing end -> the run-out table cooling spray pattern was not adjusted for the new grade's recommended cooling profile.
Why 3: Cooling profile not adjusted -> the new grade's setpoint recipe had not been loaded into the run-out table controller before the changeover.
Why 4: Recipe not loaded -> the changeover checklist references 'verify rolling parameters' but does not explicitly list run-out table cooling recipe as a separate item.

Why 5 (root cause): the grade-changeover checklist bundles cooling-recipe verification inside a generic 'rolling parameters' line item, making it easy to treat as already covered by the mill setpoint check.
root_cause: The changeover checklist does not list run-out table cooling recipe verification as its own explicit item, so it gets silently skipped under the assumption it's covered elsewhere.
corrective_action: Load the correct cooling recipe immediately; quarantine and inspect all coils since changeover start for crazing.
preventive_action: Split the changeover checklist's 'verify rolling parameters' item into separate, individually-signed sub-items, with 'run-out table cooling recipe' as its own explicit line.
effectiveness_verification: Audit the next 15 grade changeovers for checklist compliance; target zero cooling-recipe-related defects in that window.

non_conformance_description: Quality inspector on Line 2 day shift found crazing across the full width of two consecutive coils (HR-2050, HR-2051) following an unplanned rolling-speed reduction due to a downstream jam.
five_why: Why 1: Full-width crazing appeared -> the strip spent longer than normal in the high-temperature zone due to reduced line speed.
Why 2: Line speed was reduced -> a downstream coiler jam forced a temporary slowdown without adjusting furnace output.
Why 3: Furnace output was not adjusted -> there is no automated link between line-speed changes and furnace zone temperature setpoints.
Why 4: No automated link exists -> the furnace and mill speed controls were installed by different vendors on separate control systems that were never integrated.
Why 5 (root cause): the plant's furnace and rolling-line control systems operate independently, so speed disruptions are not automatically compensated by temperature adjustments.
root_cause: Furnace temperature control and rolling-line speed control are on separate, non-integrated systems, so an unplanned speed change does not trigger a compensating temperature adjustment.
corrective_action: Manually reduce furnace zone temperatures for the remainder of the slowdown; scrap or downgrade the two affected coils per grade specification.
preventive_action: Implement an interim manual SOP requiring the line operator to notify the furnace operator within 60 seconds of any speed reduction event >15%, pending longer-term integration of the two control systems (tracked as a separate capital project).
effectiveness_verification: Track all speed-reduction events over 30 days; verify furnace-operator notification occurred within 60 seconds for 100% of events, with zero resulting crazing defects.

non_conformance_description: Recurring low-level crazing (under 0.5% of coils) reported by Line 1 across three consecutive weeks, always on the same roll stand, not tied to any single shift or grade.
five_why: Why 1: Crazing recurs regardless of shift or grade -> a fixed piece of equipment is the common factor.
Why 2: The common factor is stand-4 work rolls -> the rolls show a shallow surface texture from wear that is transferring onto the strip.
Why 3: Rolls show wear texture -> the stand-4 roll change interval was extended from 3 days to 5 days six weeks ago.
Why 4: Interval was extended -> a scheduling change was made to reduce changeover downtime without re-validating roll wear life against the new interval.
Why 5 (root cause): the roll-change interval was modified based on a downtime-reduction target without a corresponding wear-life validation study.
root_cause: The stand-4 roll-change interval was extended for downtime reasons without validating that roll surface wear stays within tolerance over the new interval.
corrective_action: Revert stand-4 to the original 3-day roll-change interval immediately; inspect and replace current rolls.
preventive_action: Require any future roll-change interval modification to go through a documented wear-life validation (surface roughness measurement at proposed interval) and quality sign-off before implementation.
effectiveness_verification: Monitor stand-4 crazing rate over the next 4 weeks at reverted interval; target return to baseline (<0.1%) and zero interval changes made without validation sign-off.

non_conformance_description: Customer complaint received for coil HR-0998 (shipped 2 weeks prior) citing surface crazing discovered during their own downstream processing; internal inspection records for that coil show no defect was flagged at dispatch.
five_why: Why 1: Defect reached the customer undetected -> the crazing was below the visual detection threshold used at final inspection lighting conditions.
Why 2: Below detection threshold at final inspection -> final inspection uses standard overhead lighting, not the raking/oblique light angle needed to reveal fine crazing.
Why 3: Raking light is not used -> the final inspection station was not equipped with adjustable-angle lighting when it was set up.
Why 4: Not equipped -> the inspection station specification at installation was based on general surface-defect visibility, not defect-family-specific detection requirements.
Why 5 (root cause): the final inspection lighting specification was never updated to include oblique lighting specifically required for fine crack-type defects like crazing.
root_cause: Final inspection station lighting was specified for general defect visibility and was never updated to include the oblique/raking light angle needed to reliably detect fine crazing.
corrective_action: Notify the customer, arrange coil recall/credit per customer agreement; re-inspect recent shipments of the same grade under temporary raking-light setup.
preventive_action: Install adjustable-angle raking lighting at the final inspection station and add a documented crazing-specific inspection step to the final inspection SOP.
effectiveness_verification: Zero crazing-related customer complaints over the next 90 days; monthly internal audit confirms raking-light inspection step is being performed and documented.

non_conformance_description: Billet-cutting inspection on Caster 2 found visible non-metallic inclusions in the cross-section of 4 out of 40 billets sampled from heat H-3391.
five_why: Why 1: Inclusions found in billet cross-section -> non-metallic particles were present in the liquid steel at solidification.
Why 2: Particles were present -> refractory erosion from the tundish lining introduced material into the melt.
Why 3: Refractory eroded -> the tundish lining had exceeded its rated heat-count life before being scheduled for replacement.
Why 4: Exceeded rated life -> refractory life tracking is done manually on a paper log that was not updated for the last 3 heats.
Why 5 (root cause): tundish refractory life tracking depends on a manual paper log with no system-enforced replacement trigger, allowing it to run past rated life undetected.
root_cause: Refractory lining life is tracked manually with no automated or enforced trigger, so a lining can silently exceed its rated heat count before replacement.
corrective_action: Replace the tundish lining immediately; quarantine and section-test all billets cast on the current lining before further processing.
preventive_action: Move refractory life tracking into the caster's digital heat-count system with an automatic hold/alert when a lining approaches its rated heat count.
effectiveness_verification: Zero refractory-related inclusion defects over the next 60 heats; audit confirms 100% of relining events triggered by the digital alert rather than manual log entry.

non_conformance_description: Rolled coil from billets of heat H-3402 showed surface inclusions after hot rolling, traced back to the casting stage upon metallurgical review; affected roughly 8% of the heat's output.
five_why: Why 1: Inclusions traced to casting -> slag carryover occurred from the ladle into the tundish during pouring.
Why 2: Slag carryover occurred -> the ladle slag-detection sensor did not trigger the automatic stopper-rod cutoff.
Why 3: Sensor did not trigger -> the sensor's calibration had drifted outside acceptable tolerance.
Why 4: Calibration drifted -> the sensor calibration schedule is quarterly, and this heat fell near the end of the calibration window.

Why 5 (root cause): the slag-detection sensor calibration interval (quarterly) is longer than the sensor's demonstrated drift tolerance allows, letting sensitivity degrade before the next scheduled check.
root_cause: The quarterly slag-sensor calibration interval is too long relative to the sensor's actual drift rate, allowing detection sensitivity to degrade before recalibration.
corrective_action: Recalibrate the slag-detection sensor immediately; hold and re-sample billets from the affected heat.
preventive_action: Shorten the slag-detection sensor calibration interval from quarterly to monthly and add a mid-interval functional drift check using a reference standard.
effectiveness_verification: Track sensor drift readings monthly for 2 quarters; target drift remaining within tolerance at every check, zero slag-carryover inclusion events.

non_conformance_description: New grade trial heat H-3410 produced billets with inclusion levels above internal spec, discovered during first-article ultrasonic testing before the heat was released.
five_why: Why 1: Inclusion levels exceeded spec -> the deoxidation practice used was the standard-grade recipe, not the trial grade's requirement.
Why 2: Standard recipe was used -> the trial grade's process sheet had not been fully released to the melt-shop floor system at the time of pour.
Why 3: Process sheet not released -> the new-grade approval workflow allows metallurgy sign-off and melt-shop release to happen as parallel, not sequential, steps.
Why 4: Parallel workflow allowed the pour to proceed on default settings -> there is no system hold that blocks a trial heat from starting until the grade-specific recipe is confirmed loaded.

Why 5 (root cause): the trial-grade release workflow has no hard system block preventing a pour from starting before the grade-specific process recipe is confirmed present in the melt-shop control system.
root_cause: The new-grade release process allows metallurgical approval and control-system recipe loading to proceed independently, with no system-enforced hold linking the two before a trial pour can begin.
corrective_action: Downgrade or scrap the affected trial heat per material disposition procedure; reload the correct recipe for any remaining trial pours.
preventive_action: Add a system interlock requiring confirmed recipe-load status before a trial heat can be initiated, sequencing metallurgy sign-off ahead of melt-shop release rather than in parallel.
effectiveness_verification: Verify the interlock blocks at least one simulated mismatched-recipe attempt during commissioning test; zero trial-heat recipe mismatches over the next 10 new-grade trials.

non_conformance_description: Routine metallurgical audit found elevated inclusion counts across multiple heats over a two-week period on Caster 1, none individually severe enough to trigger real-time rejection but trending upward.
five_why: Why 1: Inclusion counts trended upward gradually -> argon stirring intensity in the ladle had been gradually reduced over several weeks.
Why 2: Stirring intensity reduced -> operators had been manually lowering the argon flow rate to reduce visible surface turbulence, believing it improved safety.
Why 3: Operators made this adjustment -> there is no documented acceptable range for argon flow rate posted at the operator station; only a single target value with no context.
Why 4: No acceptable range posted -> the ladle-treatment SOP was written assuming a fixed setpoint would always be used and never anticipated operator-driven adjustment.

Why 5 (root cause): the ladle-treatment SOP does not document why the argon flow target exists or what range is safe to deviate within, so operators self-adjusted without visibility into the inclusion-control consequence.
root_cause: The ladle-treatment SOP specifies an argon flow target without explaining its purpose or acceptable deviation range, leaving operators to make undocumented adjustments without understanding the inclusion-control tradeoff.
corrective_action: Restore argon flow to the validated target setpoint on Caster 1 immediately; review recent heats for disposition.
preventive_action: Revise the ladle-treatment SOP to state the rationale for the argon flow target and its validated acceptable range, and add flow-rate logging with a supervisor alert for any sustained deviation beyond that range.
effectiveness_verification: Inclusion count trend returns to baseline over the next 4 weeks; flow-rate log shows zero sustained deviations outside the documented range.

non_conformance_description: A single severe inclusion cluster caused a billet to fracture during subsequent hot rolling on Line 2, halting production for 40 minutes; heat H-3425 traced as the source.
five_why: Why 1: Billet fractured under rolling load -> a large inclusion cluster created a stress concentration point.
Why 2: Large cluster formed -> a refractory nozzle partially collapsed during pouring, releasing a burst of material into the stream.
Why 3: Nozzle partially collapsed -> the nozzle was from a new supplier batch that had not completed incoming inspection before use.
Why 4: Used before inspection completed -> the melt shop had run low on approved-stock nozzles and used the new batch under time pressure.
Why 5 (root cause): there is no hard hold preventing unqualified incoming refractory stock from being used when approved stock runs low, so time pressure can override the incoming-inspection gate.
root_cause: The refractory incoming-inspection process can be bypassed under production time pressure because there is no system hold preventing unqualified stock from being pulled into use.
corrective_action: Halt use of the affected nozzle batch; complete incoming inspection on remaining units before any further use; disposition the fractured billet and downstream material.
preventive_action: Implement a physical/system lockout (e.g., barcode-gated storage) that prevents refractory stock from being issued to the floor until incoming inspection is marked complete, regardless of stock-out pressure.
effectiveness_verification: Zero unqualified-refractory-use incidents over the next 90 days; storage lockout audit confirms 100% of issued stock had completed inspection.

non_conformance_description: Irregular light-colored patches observed on the top surface of coil HR-2210, Line 3, covering roughly 10% of the coil's visible surface, first noticed mid-shift.
five_why: Why 1: Light-colored patches appeared -> uneven oxide/scale formation occurred on the strip surface before descaling.
Why 2: Uneven scale formation -> furnace zone-2 burners were firing unevenly across the width.
Why 3: Uneven firing -> one burner nozzle had partial fuel-line restriction from accumulated deposits.
Why 4: Deposits accumulated -> burner nozzle cleaning is only performed during scheduled shutdowns, roughly every 8 weeks.
Why 5 (root cause): burner nozzle cleaning frequency is tied to shutdown scheduling convenience rather than to the deposit accumulation rate observed in practice.
root_cause: Burner nozzle cleaning interval is set by shutdown-schedule convenience rather than by measured deposit-accumulation rate, allowing partial restriction to develop between cleanings.
corrective_action: Clean the affected burner nozzle immediately; inspect surrounding coils for similar patching.
preventive_action: Establish a deposit-accumulation-based cleaning interval (determined by periodic flow-rate testing) independent of shutdown scheduling, with interim manual flow checks between shutdowns.
effectiveness_verification: Burner flow-rate checks show no significant restriction over next 3 monitoring cycles; zero patch-defect recurrence over 30 days.

non_conformance_description: Line 1 day shift reported dull, irregular patches on coil HR-2260 concentrated near the strip centerline, coinciding with a recent descaler header maintenance.
five_why: Why 1: Patches concentrated at centerline -> descaler spray coverage was reduced in the center zone.
Why 2: Reduced coverage -> a center-zone nozzle was reinstalled at the wrong angle after maintenance.
Why 3: Wrong angle -> the maintenance work order did not specify nozzle angle settings, only 'reinstall per standard.'
Why 4: No angle spec on work order -> nozzle angle settings are documented in a separate engineering drawing not routinely attached to maintenance work orders.
Why 5 (root cause): critical setup parameters (nozzle angle) live in a document not linked to the maintenance work order, so technicians rely on memory or approximation during reassembly.
root_cause: Descaler nozzle angle specifications exist in a separate engineering drawing that is not attached to or referenced by the maintenance work order, so correct reassembly depends on technician memory.
corrective_action: Re-angle the center-zone nozzle to specification immediately; re-inspect coils processed since the maintenance event.
preventive_action: Attach the nozzle-angle engineering drawing directly to the descaler maintenance work order template and require a photo-verification step confirming angle before sign-off.
effectiveness_verification: Zero descaler-related patch defects over next 20 maintenance-adjacent production days; work-order audit confirms drawing attachment and photo verification present.

non_conformance_description: Sporadic patch defects (roughly 1 in 50 coils) reported across Line 2 over a month, with no single obvious cause identified by operators.
five_why: Why 1: Patches occur sporadically without an obvious pattern -> incoming slab surface condition varies between suppliers.
Why 2: Slab surface condition varies -> two different slab suppliers are used interchangeably without a documented surface-quality difference in receiving records.
Why 3: No documented difference -> incoming slab inspection checks dimensional and chemical specs but not surface oxide condition.
Why 4: Surface oxide condition not checked -> the incoming inspection checklist was designed before patch-defect trending began and was never updated.

Why 5 (root cause): incoming slab inspection criteria were fixed at initial checklist design and have not been revisited to include surface oxide condition despite downstream patch-defect trends implicating it.
root_cause: Incoming slab inspection does not check surface oxide condition, a factor that trend data now implicates in patch defects, because the checklist was never revisited after initial design.
corrective_action: Add a surface oxide visual check to incoming inspection for the current slab lot; segregate slabs showing heavy oxide condition for closer monitoring.
preventive_action: Formally update the incoming slab inspection checklist to include a surface oxide condition rating, with a documented acceptance threshold agreed with both slab suppliers.
effectiveness_verification: Patch defect rate on Line 2 drops below 1 in 200 coils over the next 60 days; incoming inspection records show oxide rating captured for 100% of received slab lots.

non_conformance_description: Large single patch defect (approx. 0.3m x 0.2m) found on coil HR-2301, causing customer rejection at receiving inspection; traced to a localized event during rolling.
five_why: Why 1: Large localized patch -> a brief loss of descaler water pressure occurred during that section's pass.
Why 2: Pressure loss occurred -> the descaler pump momentarily cavitated due to a low water reservoir level.
Why 3: Reservoir was low -> the reservoir refill valve had a slow response lag under high-demand conditions.
Why 4: Slow refill response -> the refill valve had not been serviced despite showing degraded response in prior maintenance logs.

Why 5 (root cause): degraded refill valve response noted in maintenance logs was not escalated to a work order because there is no defined threshold at which a logged observation triggers mandatory action.
root_cause: There is no defined escalation threshold linking a logged 'degraded' maintenance observation to a mandatory corrective work order, so early warning signs are recorded but not acted on.
corrective_action: Service the refill valve immediately; issue customer credit/replacement per complaint procedure; inspect reservoir levels across all descaler stations.
preventive_action: Define explicit escalation thresholds in the maintenance logging system so that a 'degraded' rating on safety- or quality-critical components automatically generates a work order within a set timeframe.
effectiveness_verification: Zero unaddressed 'degraded' log entries older than the defined escalation window over the next quarter; zero recurrence of reservoir-related patch defects.

non_conformance_description: Night shift trainee flagged patch-like discoloration on coil HR-2318 but was unsure if it met the rejection threshold; coil was released and later reworked at customer's request.
five_why: Why 1: Borderline defect was released -> the trainee lacked a clear visual reference for the rejection threshold.
Why 2: No clear reference -> the plant's defect-severity reference photos are kept in a binder in the QA office, not at the inspection station.
Why 3: Reference kept off-station -> the inspection station was set up before the photo reference guide was created and was never retrofitted.
Why 4: Never retrofitted -> there is no periodic review step that checks whether inspection stations have current reference materials.
Why 5 (root cause): there is no periodic audit step confirming that visual reference materials created after station setup actually get deployed to the physical inspection stations.
root_cause: New visual defect-severity references are created centrally but there is no audit step ensuring they are physically deployed to every inspection station, so stations set up earlier remain without them.
corrective_action: Post laminated defect-severity reference photos at the Line 2 inspection station immediately; re-evaluate the released coil per customer agreement.
preventive_action: Add a quarterly audit checklist item confirming current visual reference materials are physically present and legible at every inspection station plant-wide.
effectiveness_verification: Quarterly audit shows 100% of inspection stations with current reference materials; zero borderline-defect release incidents over the following 2 quarters.

non_conformance_description: Multiple shallow pits visible on the top surface near the strip edge after descaling, batch HR-2291, Line 2 night shift, roughly 1 in 20 coils affected over two days.
five_why: Why 1: Pitting appears post-descaling -> scale was not fully removed before rolling.
Why 2: Scale removal was incomplete -> descaler spray pressure was uneven across the strip width.
Why 3: Spray pressure was uneven -> one or more descaler header nozzles were partially obstructed.
Why 4: Nozzles were obstructed -> scheduled nozzle-cleaning/filter-change was missed during the preceding maintenance window.
Why 5 (root cause): the maintenance scheduling system does not flag descaler nozzle cleaning as a hard-blocking task before shift handover, allowing it to be silently skipped under workload pressure.
root_cause: The maintenance scheduling system does not flag descaler nozzle cleaning as a hard-blocking task before shift handover, allowing it to be silently skipped under workload pressure.
corrective_action: Immediately inspect and clean all descaler header nozzles on Line 2; quarantine and re-inspect all coils produced since the start of the affected shift window before release.
preventive_action: Convert descaler nozzle inspection/cleaning into a hard-blocking checklist item in the shift-handover system that cannot be bypassed without supervisor sign-off; add a spray-pressure sensor alarm on the descaler header to flag a >=10% pressure drop in real time.
effectiveness_verification: Monitor pit-defect rate on Line 2 over the next 15 production days; target rate below 0.5% of coils, with zero missed-cleaning checklist events recorded in the handover log over the same period.

non_conformance_description: Rolled pit defects observed on coil CR-0410, isolated to a 2m section, coinciding with a work-roll change earlier in the shift.
five_why: Why 1: Rolled pits appeared after roll change -> the newly installed work roll had surface pitting from prior storage.
Why 2: Roll had storage-related pitting -> rolls are stored in a general equipment yard without corrosion-protective covering.
Why 3: No protective covering -> roll storage procedure specifies indoor storage but does not mandate covering for rolls awaiting reinstallation.
Why 4: Covering not mandated -> the storage procedure was written when all rolls were used within 48 hours, before current longer inventory cycles began.

Why 5 (root cause): the roll storage procedure was written under old inventory-cycle assumptions (fast turnover) that no longer match current practice, so it lacks corrosion protection requirements needed for longer storage durations.
root_cause: The roll storage procedure predates the plant's current longer roll-inventory cycles and was never updated to require corrosion protection for rolls held longer than the original 48-hour assumption.
corrective_action: Remove and inspect the current work roll; replace with a roll confirmed free of surface pitting; disposition the affected 2m section.
preventive_action: Update the roll storage procedure to mandate corrosion-protective covering and a maximum uncovered storage duration, with a pre-installation surface inspection step for any roll stored over 7 days.
effectiveness_verification: Zero storage-related rolled pit defects over next 10 roll changes; storage audit confirms 100% of rolls in inventory have protective covering.

non_conformance_description: Pitting defect cluster found during in-process inspection on Line 4, associated with a change to a new coolant supplier three weeks prior.
five_why: Why 1: Pitting cluster appeared -> localized micro-corrosion occurred on the strip surface during rolling.
Why 2: Micro-corrosion occurred -> the new coolant's corrosion-inhibitor concentration was lower than the previous supplier's formulation.
Why 3: Lower inhibitor concentration -> the new coolant was approved based on lubricity and cost criteria without a corrosion-inhibitor equivalence test.
Why 4: No equivalence test performed -> the supplier-change approval process for consumables does not require corrosion-performance testing, only lubricity and cost review.

Why 5 (root cause): the consumable supplier-change approval process evaluates lubricity and cost but has no required corrosion-inhibitor equivalence test, so a formulation difference in a non-evaluated property was missed.
root_cause: The supplier-change approval process for rolling coolant does not include a required corrosion-inhibitor equivalence test, so relevant formulation differences can pass approval unnoticed.
corrective_action: Revert to the previous coolant supplier or formulation while the new one is re-evaluated; inspect and disposition affected coils from the last 3 weeks.
preventive_action: Add a mandatory corrosion-inhibitor equivalence test to the consumable supplier-change approval checklist for any coolant/lubricant substitution.
effectiveness_verification: Coolant re-approval includes documented corrosion test results before reintroduction; zero coolant-related pitting defects over the next 30 days post-reintroduction.

non_conformance_description: Isolated pitting found on coil CR-0455 traced to a single roll bite event; equipment logs show a momentary tension drop at the same timestamp.
five_why: Why 1: Pitting at a specific point -> a momentary loss of strip tension caused contact irregularity between strip and roll.
Why 2: Tension loss occurred -> the tension control system's feedback sensor had a brief signal dropout.
Why 3: Signal dropout occurred -> a loose connector on the sensor cable had intermittent contact.
Why 4: Connector was loose -> the cable routing passes through a high-vibration zone without strain relief.
Why 5 (root cause): the tension sensor cable was routed through a high-vibration area without strain relief hardware, allowing vibration to gradually loosen the connector over time.
root_cause: The tension sensor cable lacks strain relief in a high-vibration routing zone, allowing the connector to loosen gradually until it caused an intermittent signal dropout.
corrective_action: Secure/replace the loose connector immediately; inspect the affected coil section and disposition per spec.
preventive_action: Add strain-relief hardware to the tension sensor cable routing and include cable connector integrity as a check item in the preventive maintenance schedule for that zone.
effectiveness_verification: Zero tension-related sensor dropouts over next 90 days; PM records confirm connector checks performed on schedule.

non_conformance_description: Cluster of pitting defects found plant-wide across multiple lines over a single week, coinciding with an announced water-treatment plant maintenance event.
five_why: Why 1: Pitting occurred across multiple lines simultaneously -> a shared input changed for all lines at once.
Why 2: Shared input changed -> process water pH shifted outside normal range during water-treatment plant maintenance.
Why 3: pH shifted -> the water-treatment team did not notify production of the maintenance window or its expected water-quality impact.
Why 4: No notification given -> there is no formal communication protocol between the utilities/water-treatment team and production quality for planned maintenance affecting shared process inputs.

Why 5 (root cause): no formal cross-functional notification protocol exists between utilities maintenance and production quality for planned work that affects shared process inputs like water quality.
root_cause: There is no formal notification protocol requiring the utilities/water-treatment team to alert production quality before planned maintenance that could affect shared process inputs such as water pH.
corrective_action: Restore process water to spec; inspect and disposition affected production across all lines from the maintenance window.
preventive_action: Establish a formal cross-functional notification protocol requiring utilities to notify production quality at least 24 hours before any planned maintenance affecting shared process inputs, with a defined escalation contact.
effectiveness_verification: 100% of subsequent utilities maintenance events show documented 24-hour advance notification over the next 2 quarters; zero water-quality-related multi-line defect events.

non_conformance_description: Embedded scale pattern found across the width of coil HR-2410, Line 1, first noticed at final visual inspection; no in-process alarm triggered.
five_why: Why 1: Scale is embedded across full width -> descaler was not active during that pass.
Why 2: Descaler was not active -> the descaler was left in standby mode after a prior grade change that did not require descaling.
Why 3: Left in standby -> there is no automatic default-to-active state for the descaler between grade changes.
Why 4: No automatic default -> the descaler control was designed assuming operators would always manually re-enable it, without a fail-safe default.
Why 5 (root cause): the descaler control system has no fail-safe default-to-active state, relying entirely on manual operator re-enablement after any standby period.
root_cause: The descaler control system defaults to whatever state it was last left in rather than fail-safing to active, so a standby setting from a prior grade silently carries over to the next run.
corrective_action: Re-enable the descaler immediately; quarantine and downgrade the affected coil.
preventive_action: Reconfigure the descaler control logic to default to active at the start of every new coil/heat, requiring explicit operator confirmation to enter standby rather than to exit it.
effectiveness_verification: Zero descaler-standby-related scale defects over next 30 production days; control logic audit confirms default-active behavior verified in test.

non_conformance_description: Localized rolled-in scale patches on coil HR-2455, appearing intermittently rather than continuously, Line 3.
five_why: Why 1: Scale appears intermittently -> descaler spray pressure fluctuates rather than staying constant.
Why 2: Pressure fluctuates -> the descaler pump's pressure regulator is aging and no longer holds a stable setpoint.
Why 3: Regulator is aging -> it is past its manufacturer-recommended service life but has no replacement scheduled.
Why 4: No replacement scheduled -> the plant's preventive maintenance plan does not include a defined service-life-based replacement schedule for this component class.
Why 5 (root cause): the preventive maintenance plan tracks failure-based repair for pressure regulators but has no proactive service-life-based replacement schedule for this component class.
root_cause: The preventive maintenance plan lacks a service-life-based replacement schedule for descaler pressure regulators, so aging units are only addressed reactively after failure symptoms appear.
corrective_action: Replace the aging pressure regulator immediately; inspect recent coils for intermittent scale patterns.
preventive_action: Add descaler pressure regulators to the PM plan with a proactive, service-life-based replacement schedule per manufacturer recommendation, rather than run-to-failure.
effectiveness_verification: Pressure stability logs show setpoint held within tolerance over next 60 days; zero intermittent scale defects in that window.

non_conformance_description: Coil HR-2470 showed rolled-in scale concentrated at the leading edge only, Line 2 morning shift, first coil after a cold start following a weekend shutdown.
five_why: Why 1: Scale concentrated at leading edge only -> descaler water was not yet at operating pressure when the leading edge passed through.
Why 2: Water not at pressure -> the descaler pump takes several minutes to reach full pressure after a cold start.
Why 3: Pump not pre-started -> the startup checklist sequences descaler activation after, not before, strip threading.
Why 4: Sequencing is after threading -> the checklist was written around minimizing water usage during idle periods rather than around descaler readiness timing.

Why 5 (root cause): the startup checklist sequence was optimized for water conservation during idle time rather than for ensuring descaler pressure readiness before the leading edge reaches the descaler.
root_cause: The startup checklist sequences descaler pump activation after strip threading (to conserve water during idle time), which does not allow enough lead time for the pump to reach operating pressure before the leading edge passes through.
corrective_action: Trim and downgrade the affected leading-edge section; re-sequence remaining startup for this shift to pre-start the descaler.
preventive_action: Revise the startup checklist to activate the descaler pump a defined lead time (based on measured pressure ramp-up) before strip threading begins, accepting the minor water-usage tradeoff.
effectiveness_verification: Zero leading-edge scale defects over the next 10 cold-start events; pressure logs confirm operating pressure reached before threading in each case.

non_conformance_description: Scale defect found on a single coil (HR-2481) traced to an operator manually bypassing the descaler for a rush order to save cycle time.
five_why: Why 1: Descaler was bypassed -> the operator manually disabled it to meet a rush delivery deadline.
Why 2: Operator felt able to bypass it -> the descaler bypass function is accessible without any supervisory authorization or system log entry.
Why 3: No authorization required -> the bypass control was originally added for maintenance testing purposes, not intended for production use, but was never access-restricted.
Why 4: Never access-restricted -> when the bypass feature was added, there was no formal review of its production-floor access implications.

Why 5 (root cause): the descaler bypass function, added for maintenance testing, was never access-restricted or logged, leaving it available for undocumented use during production under schedule pressure.
root_cause: The descaler bypass control, intended only for maintenance testing, was never access-restricted or logged, making it available for unauthorized production-floor use under schedule pressure.
corrective_action: Downgrade or scrap the affected coil; counsel the operator per standard practice and communicate the schedule-pressure concern to supervision for resolution.
preventive_action: Restrict the descaler bypass function to supervisor-level access with mandatory system logging of every activation, including a required reason code.
effectiveness_verification: Bypass activation log shows zero unauthorized uses over next 90 days; 100% of legitimate maintenance bypasses have reason codes logged.

non_conformance_description: Low-level rolled-in scale (isolated spots, not continuous) found sporadically across Line 1 over two months, no clear correlation with shift, grade, or equipment identified by initial investigation.
five_why: Why 1: Sporadic isolated spots with no clear correlation -> descaler nozzles intermittently clog with fine debris rather than fully blocking.
Why 2: Intermittent clogging -> incoming descaler water is not filtered finely enough to catch the fine particulate causing partial clogs.

Why 3: Filtration insufficient -> the water filtration system's mesh size was specified based on the original 1990s equipment generation and was never updated when nozzles were upgraded to finer-spray models.
Why 4: Never updated -> equipment upgrades (nozzles) and utility specifications (filtration) are managed by separate teams without a cross-check step at upgrade time.

Why 5 (root cause): nozzle upgrades and water filtration specifications are managed by separate teams with no cross-check step, so a nozzle upgrade to finer spray tolerances was never matched with a corresponding filtration upgrade.
root_cause: Equipment upgrades (descaler nozzles) and utility specifications (water filtration mesh size) are managed by separate teams with no cross-check step at upgrade time, so filtration was never matched to the finer nozzle tolerances introduced years ago.
corrective_action: Add an interim finer in-line filter ahead of the descaler header on Line 1; flush and inspect current nozzles for partial clogs.
preventive_action: Establish a cross-functional sign-off requirement between equipment engineering and utilities whenever nozzle/spray equipment is upgraded, explicitly checking upstream filtration compatibility.
effectiveness_verification: Sporadic scale defect rate drops to near zero over the next 60 days; documented cross-check sign-off present for the next equipment upgrade as a process test.

non_conformance_description: Linear scratches found on multiple coils during final packaging inspection, Line 2, all oriented the same direction consistent with handling equipment contact.
five_why: Why 1: Consistent-direction linear scratches -> the coil is contacting a fixed guide surface during transfer to packaging.
Why 2: Contact with guide surface -> a transfer roller's protective sleeve has worn through, exposing bare metal.
Why 3: Sleeve worn through -> sleeve wear inspection is visual-only and was scheduled but missed during the last two rounds.
Why 4: Inspection missed -> the sleeve inspection task is not tracked in the digital maintenance system, only on a paper rotation sheet.
Why 5 (root cause): sleeve inspection tasks live on a manual paper rotation sheet outside the digital maintenance tracking system, making missed inspections invisible to the compliance dashboard.
root_cause: Transfer roller sleeve inspection is tracked on a manual paper sheet outside the digital maintenance system, so missed inspections are not visible on the compliance dashboard and go unnoticed.
corrective_action: Replace the worn roller sleeve immediately; inspect coils processed since the sleeve wear likely began.
preventive_action: Migrate transfer roller sleeve inspection into the digital maintenance tracking system with the same missed-task alerting used for other critical PM items.
effectiveness_verification: Zero missed sleeve inspections over next 90 days per digital system records; zero recurrence of transfer-roller scratch defects.

non_conformance_description: Single deep scratch found on coil FN-0512 during customer receiving inspection; internal records show no defect flagged before shipment.
five_why: Why 1: Deep scratch reached customer undetected -> the defect occurred during loading, after the final quality inspection point.
Why 2: Occurred after inspection -> the loading dock crane's coil sling made direct metal-to-metal contact during transfer.
Why 3: Direct metal contact -> the protective sling padding had not been replaced despite visible wear noted by the dock crew informally.
Why 4: Not replaced despite informal notice -> there is no formal reporting channel for dock crew to flag equipment condition issues to maintenance; concerns are passed verbally and can be lost.

Why 5 (root cause): dock crew equipment-condition concerns are communicated informally with no formal reporting channel, so a known padding-wear issue was never converted into a tracked maintenance action.
root_cause: There is no formal reporting channel for loading-dock crew to flag equipment condition concerns to maintenance, so informally-raised issues (like sling padding wear) are not tracked or actioned.
corrective_action: Replace the sling padding immediately; process the customer complaint per procedure (credit/replacement); inspect other slings plant-wide.
preventive_action: Create a simple formal reporting channel (e.g., a logged tag-out or digital form) for floor/dock staff to flag equipment condition concerns, feeding directly into the maintenance work-order queue.
effectiveness_verification: Zero loading-related scratch complaints over next quarter; reporting channel shows active use with tracked resolution times.

non_conformance_description: Recurring fine scratches noted by quality on Line 4 across a shift, all short and randomly oriented, not matching any single equipment contact point.
five_why: Why 1: Random short scratches with no single contact point -> loose metallic debris is present on a contact surface, causing intermittent scoring.
Why 2: Debris present -> housekeeping/cleaning of the finishing line contact surfaces is done at end-of-shift only, not during the shift.
Why 3: Cleaning only at end-of-shift -> the cleaning SOP was designed around the original single-shift operation and never updated for the plant's current 3-shift continuous operation.
Why 4: Never updated for 3-shift operation -> SOP revision typically happens reactively when a specific incident triggers review, and no incident had previously been traced to this cause.

Why 5 (root cause): the finishing line cleaning SOP still reflects single-shift-era assumptions and was never revisited when the plant moved to continuous 3-shift operation, since SOP updates are triggered reactively rather than by operational-change review.
root_cause: The finishing line cleaning SOP was written for single-shift operation and was never revisited when the plant moved to continuous 3-shift operation, since SOPs are only updated reactively after an incident, not proactively when operations change.
corrective_action: Perform an immediate mid-shift cleaning of contact surfaces on Line 4; inspect coils processed since the last cleaning.
preventive_action: Revise the cleaning SOP to include mid-shift cleaning cycles matched to the current 3-shift operating pattern, and add a trigger requiring SOP review whenever operating patterns (shift structure, line speed, etc.) change.
effectiveness_verification: Debris-related scratch defect rate drops to near zero over next 30 days; SOP revision log shows the new operational-change review trigger documented.

non_conformance_description: Scratches found concentrated on the underside of coils only, Line 3, coinciding with the introduction of a new coil-turning device two weeks prior.
five_why: Why 1: Scratches only on underside -> the new coil-turning device contacts the underside surface during rotation.
Why 2: Device contacts surface -> the turning device's contact pads were specified for a different (thicker gauge) product than currently running.
Why 3: Pads specified for wrong gauge -> the equipment procurement spec referenced the plant's most common historical product mix, not the current mix which has shifted toward thinner gauges.
Why 4: Spec based on historical mix -> there was no product-mix review step in the equipment procurement process to check against current/forecasted production.

Why 5 (root cause): the equipment procurement process specifies contact components based on historical product mix without a required check against current or forecasted product mix at time of purchase.
root_cause: Equipment procurement specifications were based on historical product mix without a required check against the current/forecasted product mix, so contact pads suited to thicker gauge were installed for a plant now running thinner gauges more often.
corrective_action: Replace the turning device contact pads with a gauge-appropriate variant; inspect coils processed since installation.
preventive_action: Add a mandatory current/forecasted product-mix review step to the equipment procurement checklist for any component specified against product dimensions.
effectiveness_verification: Zero turning-device-related scratches over next 30 days with new pads installed; procurement checklist audit confirms product-mix review documented for next equipment purchase.

non_conformance_description: Isolated scratch complaint from a single customer order, traced to in-transit handling rather than plant-internal cause, following root-cause review with the logistics partner.
five_why: Why 1: Scratch present at customer receiving -> damage occurred during third-party transport, not at the plant.
Why 2: Damage occurred in transport -> the coil was loaded without the agreed protective wrap specified in the shipping instruction.
Why 3: Protective wrap omitted -> the shipping instruction was attached to the order documentation but not physically present at the loading bay for the third-party carrier's crew.

Why 4: Not present at loading bay -> shipping instructions are emailed to the logistics coordinator but not printed/posted at the physical loading point for carrier crews who may not have email access.

Why 5 (root cause): shipping/packaging instructions are distributed digitally to the logistics coordinator only, with no requirement that they be physically present at the loading bay for third-party carrier crews to reference.
root_cause: Shipping and packaging instructions are distributed only via email to the internal logistics coordinator, with no requirement that they be physically posted at the loading bay where third-party carrier crews, who may lack email access, actually load the product.
corrective_action: Process the customer complaint per procedure; notify the logistics partner of the gap for this shipment and confirm corrective packaging on any remaining order quantity.
preventive_action: Require a printed/posted copy of shipping and packaging instructions at the physical loading bay for every order, verified by the logistics coordinator before loading begins, independent of the digital record.
effectiveness_verification: Zero transport-related scratch complaints traced to missing wrap over the next quarter; loading bay audit confirms physical instructions present for a sample of outbound orders.

non_conformance_description: Half-circle-shaped material loss defect found at the trailing edge of sheared sheets from Line 4 shear station, roughly 1 in 30 sheets affected over the shift.
five_why: Why 1: Crescent-shaped gap at trailing edge -> the shear blade made an incomplete, curved cut rather than a clean straight cut.
Why 2: Incomplete curved cut -> the shear blade has localized wear at the specific contact point corresponding to this sheet length.
Why 3: Localized wear at that point -> the shear has been running the same sheet length repeatedly for an extended run without lateral blade-position rotation.
Why 4: No lateral rotation performed -> the shear maintenance SOP does not include a periodic blade-position rotation step to distribute wear.

Why 5 (root cause): the shear maintenance SOP has no periodic blade-position rotation requirement, so extended runs at a fixed cut length concentrate wear at a single contact point instead of distributing it.
root_cause: The shear maintenance SOP has no periodic blade-position rotation step, so long runs at a single cut length concentrate blade wear at one contact point rather than distributing it across the blade.
corrective_action: Rotate or replace the shear blade at the worn position immediately; inspect and disposition affected sheets from the current run.
preventive_action: Add a periodic blade-position rotation step to the shear maintenance SOP, triggered by cumulative cut count at a fixed length rather than calendar time alone.
effectiveness_verification: Zero crescent gap defects over next 5,000 cuts at the same length; blade wear measurement confirms more even wear distribution at next scheduled inspection.

non_conformance_description: Crescent gap defects appeared suddenly on Line 4 shear after a blade replacement earlier in the shift, affecting the first several sheets post-replacement.
five_why: Why 1: Defects appeared right after blade replacement -> the new blade was not aligned to the correct gap tolerance during installation.
Why 2: Alignment was incorrect -> the alignment gauge used was not the current calibrated version.
Why 3: Wrong gauge used -> a superseded gauge from a prior tooling generation was still present in the toolbox alongside the current one.
Why 4: Superseded gauge still present -> there is no formal process for removing/red-tagging obsolete tooling when a replacement gauge is introduced.
Why 5 (root cause): obsolete alignment gauges are not formally removed or red-tagged when replacement tooling is introduced, leaving superseded tools available for accidental use.
root_cause: There is no formal process for removing or red-tagging obsolete alignment gauges when replacement tooling is introduced, so a superseded gauge remained available in the toolbox and was used by mistake.
corrective_action: Re-align the blade using the correct current gauge; inspect and disposition the affected first-run sheets.
preventive_action: Implement a formal red-tag/removal process for obsolete tooling whenever a replacement is introduced, with toolbox audits to confirm only current-generation tools remain accessible.
effectiveness_verification: Zero misalignment incidents traced to obsolete tooling over next 90 days; toolbox audit confirms no superseded gauges present.

non_conformance_description: Gradually worsening crescent gap severity noted across a full week on Line 4, not tied to any single maintenance event.
five_why: Why 1: Gradually worsening defect -> shear blade clearance is slowly increasing over time.
Why 2: Clearance increasing -> the blade mounting bolts are gradually loosening under repeated shear-impact vibration.
Why 3: Bolts loosening -> standard (non-locking) fasteners are used at the blade mount, with no vibration-resistant hardware.
Why 4: Non-locking fasteners used -> the original equipment specification predates the plant's current higher shear cycle rate, which increased vibration loading beyond original design assumptions.

Why 5 (root cause): the shear blade mount uses standard non-locking fasteners specified under an older, lower cycle-rate assumption, and the hardware was never upgraded when the plant's cycle rate increased.
root_cause: Standard non-locking fasteners at the shear blade mount were specified under an older, lower cycle-rate assumption and were never upgraded to vibration-resistant hardware when the plant's shear cycle rate increased.
corrective_action: Re-torque blade mounting bolts to spec immediately; inspect and disposition affected sheets from the degrading-severity window.
preventive_action: Upgrade shear blade mount fasteners to vibration-resistant (e.g., nylon-insert or spring-lock) hardware rated for the current cycle rate, and add bolt-torque verification to the PM schedule.
effectiveness_verification: Torque-check logs show mounting bolts holding spec over next 60 days; zero progressive crescent-gap-severity trends observed.

non_conformance_description: New operator on Line 4 produced a batch of sheets with crescent gap defects during their first solo shift on the shear station.
five_why: Why 1: New operator's batch shows defects -> the operator set an incorrect blade gap for the material thickness being run.
Why 2: Incorrect gap set -> the operator was not aware the gap setting must change per material thickness, not just per product length.
Why 3: Not aware of thickness dependency -> the training program covers length-setting procedure in detail but only briefly mentions thickness-dependent gap adjustment.
Why 4: Training under-covers this -> the training curriculum was developed primarily around the most common product thickness run at the time, and was not revised as thickness variety increased.

Why 5 (root cause): the shear operator training curriculum under-emphasizes thickness-dependent gap adjustment because it was developed when thickness variety was lower and was never revised as the product mix diversified.
root_cause: The shear operator training curriculum was developed when the plant ran a narrower range of material thicknesses and under-emphasizes thickness-dependent blade gap adjustment; it was never revised as thickness variety in the product mix increased.
corrective_action: Correct the blade gap setting for the current material; inspect and disposition the affected batch; have a qualified operator review the remainder of the shift's output.
preventive_action: Revise the shear operator training curriculum to give thickness-dependent gap adjustment equal emphasis to length setting, including a hands-on competency check across at least 3 representative thicknesses before solo certification.
effectiveness_verification: Zero thickness-related crescent gap defects from newly certified operators over next 6 months; training records show updated curriculum delivered and competency-checked.

non_conformance_description: Crescent gap defects found only on sheets from a specific coil (source coil CR-0620), not on adjacent coils processed on the same shear the same day.
five_why: Why 1: Defects isolated to one source coil -> that coil's material hardness was outside the shear's validated range.
Why 2: Hardness outside range -> the coil came from a heat that had a documented hardness deviation, flagged at an earlier stage but not carried forward.
Why 3: Deviation not carried forward -> the hardness flag from the casting/rolling stage is recorded in the metallurgical system but not linked to the coil ID used on the shear floor.
Why 4: Systems not linked -> the metallurgical tracking system and the shop-floor coil tracking system were implemented separately and were never integrated to pass forward quality flags.

Why 5 (root cause): the metallurgical quality tracking system and the shop-floor coil tracking system are not integrated, so upstream quality flags (like a hardness deviation) do not automatically follow the coil ID to downstream operations like shearing.
root_cause: The metallurgical quality tracking system and the shop-floor coil tracking system are not integrated, so an upstream hardness deviation flag did not automatically follow the coil ID forward to the shear station, where it would have prompted a gap-setting adjustment.
corrective_action: Isolate and disposition remaining material from the flagged coil; adjust shear gap setting appropriately if the coil is still to be processed.
preventive_action: Integrate the metallurgical quality tracking system with the shop-floor coil tracking system (or implement an interim manual flag-transfer step) so upstream quality deviations are visible at every downstream operation referencing that coil ID.
effectiveness_verification: Zero downstream defects traced to un-forwarded upstream quality flags over the next 90 days; system integration (or interim process) verified functional via test case.

non_conformance_description: Visible folds/wrinkles found at the waist section of forged components from Press 2, affecting roughly 5% of the day's output, associated with a recent die change.
five_why: Why 1: Folds appear at waist section -> excessive local material deformation occurred during die fill.
Why 2: Excessive deformation -> the newly installed die had a slightly different fillet radius than the previous validated die.
Why 3: Different fillet radius -> the replacement die was machined from an updated drawing revision that was not cross-checked against the validated forging parameters.
Why 4: Not cross-checked -> die drawing revisions and forging parameter validation are managed as separate approval workflows with no linkage requirement.

Why 5 (root cause): die drawing revision approval and forging process parameter validation are handled as separate, unlinked workflows, so a geometry change (fillet radius) was not automatically flagged for re-validation against existing forging parameters.
root_cause: Die drawing revisions and forging process parameter validation are approved through separate, unlinked workflows, so a geometry change like fillet radius does not automatically trigger re-validation of the forging parameters that depend on it.
corrective_action: Revert to the previous validated die or adjust forging parameters for the new fillet radius; disposition affected components.
preventive_action: Link the die drawing revision approval workflow to a mandatory forging-parameter re-validation step whenever die geometry changes, before the new die is released to production.
effectiveness_verification: Zero waist folding defects over next 500 forged components with the new die; process audit confirms re-validation step completed and documented for the die.

non_conformance_description: Waist folding defects appeared intermittently on Press 3 across a shift, with severity varying part to part rather than being consistent.
five_why: Why 1: Severity varies part to part -> billet preheat temperature is inconsistent between parts.
Why 2: Preheat inconsistent -> the induction heater's temperature uniformity has degraded.
Why 3: Uniformity degraded -> one of the induction coil sections has partial insulation breakdown, reducing localized heating efficiency.
Why 4: Insulation breakdown undetected -> the induction heater's condition monitoring only checks overall output power, not zone-by-zone temperature uniformity.

Why 5 (root cause): induction heater condition monitoring tracks only total output power, not zone-by-zone temperature uniformity, so a localized insulation breakdown affecting one coil section goes undetected while overall power reads normal.
root_cause: The induction heater's condition monitoring only tracks total output power, not zone-by-zone temperature uniformity, so a localized insulation breakdown in one coil section goes undetected as long as overall power output appears normal.
corrective_action: Repair or replace the affected induction coil section; inspect and disposition parts forged during the degraded-uniformity period.
preventive_action: Upgrade induction heater condition monitoring to include zone-by-zone temperature measurement (e.g., multi-point pyrometry) rather than relying on total output power alone.
effectiveness_verification: Zone temperature logs show uniform heating within tolerance across all zones over next 30 days; zero preheat-related waist folding defects in that window.

non_conformance_description: A batch of components from Press 2 showed waist folding traced to an incorrect billet size being fed into the press.
five_why: Why 1: Incorrect billet size fed -> a billet from a different product's cut schedule was mixed into the current run's staging area.
Why 2: Mixed into staging -> billets for multiple upcoming product runs are staged in a shared area without size-specific segregation.
Why 3: No segregation -> the staging area layout was designed when the plant ran fewer concurrent product variants.
Why 4: Layout not updated -> facility layout changes require a capital-request process that has a long lead time, so informal workarounds (shared staging) developed instead.

Why 5 (root cause): the billet staging area layout, designed for fewer concurrent product variants, was never updated to add size-specific segregation because facility layout changes go through a slow capital-request process, leaving shared, unsegregated staging as the ongoing informal workaround.
root_cause: The billet staging area lacks size-specific segregation because updating the physical layout requires a slow capital-request process, so mixed staging has persisted as an informal workaround even as the plant's product variant count grew.
corrective_action: Sort and segregate the current staging area by billet size immediately; inspect and disposition the affected batch.
preventive_action: Implement a low-cost interim segregation measure (labeled bins/floor markings) for billet staging pending the longer-term capital-approved layout change, with a written procedure requiring segregated staging regardless of layout constraints.
effectiveness_verification: Zero billet-mix-related defects over next 90 days; staging area audit confirms segregation markings and procedure compliance.

non_conformance_description: Waist folding severity increased noticeably after a recent press-speed increase intended to improve throughput on Press 1.
five_why: Why 1: Severity increased after speed change -> higher press speed reduced the time available for material flow into the die cavity before deformation.
Why 2: Reduced flow time caused folding -> the speed increase was approved based on throughput targets without a die-fill simulation check at the new speed.
Why 3: No die-fill check performed -> the throughput improvement project's approval criteria focused on cycle time and equipment capability, not on forming-quality risk.
Why 4: Quality risk not in approval criteria -> the throughput-improvement project template does not include a required forming-quality impact assessment step.

Why 5 (root cause): the throughput-improvement project approval template has no required forming-quality impact assessment step, so a speed change can be approved based solely on cycle-time and equipment-capability criteria.
root_cause: The throughput-improvement project approval template does not require a forming-quality impact assessment, so process speed changes can be approved based only on cycle-time and equipment-capability criteria, without checking their effect on material flow and defect risk.
corrective_action: Reduce press speed back toward the previous validated rate; disposition affected components produced at the higher speed.
preventive_action: Add a mandatory forming-quality impact assessment (including die-fill simulation or trial-run defect-rate check) to the throughput-improvement project approval template for any process speed change.
effectiveness_verification: Any future speed change shows documented quality impact assessment before approval; zero waist folding defects at the re-validated speed over next 500 parts.

non_conformance_description: Waist folding found on parts forged using a lubricant lot that was recently changed due to a supplier shortage, Press 3.
five_why: Why 1: Folding appeared with new lubricant lot -> the substitute lubricant has different flow/friction characteristics, affecting material movement in the die.
Why 2: Different characteristics -> the substitute lubricant was sourced as an emergency measure during a supplier shortage without a formal equivalence trial.
Why 3: No equivalence trial performed -> emergency substitutions are handled outside the normal supplier/material change process, which is designed for planned changes with lead time.
Why 4: No emergency-substitution process exists -> the material change approval process assumes advance notice and does not define an expedited-but-still-controlled path for shortage situations.

Why 5 (root cause): the material/supplier change approval process only defines a path for planned changes with advance notice, with no expedited-but-controlled equivalence check defined for emergency shortage substitutions.
root_cause: The material change approval process only accounts for planned substitutions with advance lead time; it has no defined expedited-but-controlled equivalence check for emergency shortage situations, so the substitute lubricant went into production without a formal check.
corrective_action: Revert to the original lubricant if available, or perform an expedited friction/flow check on the substitute before continued use; disposition affected components.
preventive_action: Define an expedited (e.g., 24-48 hour) equivalence-check path within the material change approval process specifically for emergency shortage substitutions, covering the minimum critical properties (friction/flow for lubricants) rather than skipping evaluation entirely.
effectiveness_verification: Next emergency substitution event shows documented expedited equivalence check completed before use; zero lubricant-substitution-related folding defects going forward.

non_conformance_description: Incomplete fusion detected at a coil-to-coil weld joint during continuous line processing, causing an unplanned line stop when the joint failed under tension, Line 1.
five_why: Why 1: Weld joint failed under tension -> the weld had incomplete fusion across part of the joint width.
Why 2: Incomplete fusion occurred -> welding current was below the setpoint required for the current strip thickness.
Why 3: Current below setpoint -> the welder's parameter recipe had not been updated when the line began processing a new, thinner gauge range.
Why 4: Recipe not updated -> gauge-range changes are communicated to rolling/finishing teams but the welding station is not on the standard gauge-change notification list.

Why 5 (root cause): the welding station is not included on the standard notification list for gauge-range changes, so its parameter recipe was not updated when the plant began processing a new thinner gauge range.
root_cause: The coil-welding station is not included on the standard gauge-range-change notification list used to update process parameters elsewhere in the plant, so its weld recipe was not updated for the new thinner gauge range.
corrective_action: Update the welder parameter recipe for the current gauge range immediately; inspect welds made since the gauge range change for fusion quality.
preventive_action: Add the coil-welding station to the standard gauge-range-change notification list, with a required parameter recipe update and verification weld test before resuming production after any gauge-range change.
effectiveness_verification: Zero weld-related line stops over next 60 days; verification weld test on file for every subsequent gauge-range change.

non_conformance_description: Weld joint offset (misalignment) detected downstream during rolling, causing localized thickness variation and downgrade of the affected section, Line 2.
five_why: Why 1: Downstream thickness variation -> the weld joint was misaligned laterally when the two coil ends were joined.
Why 2: Lateral misalignment -> the automatic edge-alignment guide at the welder was not engaged for this joint.
Why 3: Guide not engaged -> the operator manually aligned by eye because the automatic guide had a known intermittent fault reported the previous week.
Why 4: Known fault not yet fixed -> the reported fault was logged as low-priority since manual alignment was seen as an acceptable interim workaround.

Why 5 (root cause): the known intermittent fault on the automatic edge-alignment guide was classified as low-priority because manual alignment was treated as an acceptable interim workaround, without a documented tolerance comparison showing manual alignment could not reliably meet the same precision.
root_cause: The automatic edge-alignment guide fault was classified as low-priority based on an assumption that manual alignment was an acceptable interim workaround, without verifying that manual alignment could actually meet the same tolerance as the automatic guide.
corrective_action: Repair the automatic edge-alignment guide; downgrade the affected section per thickness-variation spec; re-verify alignment on subsequent welds until repair is complete.
preventive_action: Require fault-priority classification for alignment-critical equipment to include a documented tolerance comparison against the proposed manual workaround before being downgraded to low-priority.
effectiveness_verification: Zero weld-alignment-related thickness downgrades over next 60 days; fault-priority audit confirms tolerance comparison documented for the next similar fault classification.

non_conformance_description: Weld joint thickness variation exceeded spec on a joint made during a shift-change handover, Line 1.
five_why: Why 1: Thickness variation exceeded spec -> weld pressure setting was inconsistent with the intended recipe.
Why 2: Pressure inconsistent -> the incoming shift operator did not confirm the outgoing operator's in-progress weld parameters before taking over.
Why 3: No confirmation performed -> the shift handover checklist for the welding station does not include a parameter-confirmation step, only equipment-status items.
Why 4: Parameter confirmation missing from checklist -> the handover checklist was adapted from a general equipment-status template not specific to welding-parameter-sensitive stations.

Why 5 (root cause): the welding station shift-handover checklist was adapted from a generic equipment-status template and was never customized to include weld-parameter confirmation, a step specific to the sensitivity of this station.
root_cause: The welding station's shift-handover checklist is a generic equipment-status template that was never customized to include weld-parameter confirmation, a step specifically needed for this parameter-sensitive station.
corrective_action: Re-set weld pressure to the correct recipe value; disposition the affected joint's downstream material.
preventive_action: Customize the welding station's shift-handover checklist to include explicit weld-parameter confirmation (pressure, current, timing) in addition to general equipment status.
effectiveness_verification: Zero handover-related weld parameter deviations over next 30 shift changes; handover checklist audit confirms parameter confirmation step completed each time.

non_conformance_description: Weld defect found during scheduled destructive testing of a sample joint, not causing a line stop but indicating a systemic quality drift over the past month's welds.
five_why: Why 1: Systemic drift found in sampled joints -> weld electrode condition has gradually degraded across the sampling period.
Why 2: Electrode condition degraded -> electrode replacement is based on a fixed cycle count that assumes uniform wear, but actual wear varies with the gauge range being welded.
Why 3: Fixed cycle count assumption -> the replacement schedule was set using wear data from a single reference gauge, not validated across the plant's full gauge range.
Why 4: Not validated across full range -> the original electrode life study only tested the most common gauge at the time and was not repeated as gauge variety expanded.

Why 5 (root cause): the electrode replacement schedule is based on a wear-life study conducted on a single reference gauge and was never re-validated as the plant's gauge-range variety expanded, so actual wear now varies from the assumption across different gauges.
root_cause: The weld electrode replacement schedule is based on a wear-life study conducted on a single reference gauge that was never re-validated as the plant's product gauge-range variety expanded, so the fixed cycle-count assumption no longer matches actual wear across the current gauge range.
corrective_action: Inspect and replace electrodes showing wear beyond tolerance immediately; expand destructive-test sampling temporarily to characterize the current drift extent.
preventive_action: Re-validate the electrode wear-life study across the plant's current full gauge range and set a gauge-range-adjusted replacement schedule rather than a single fixed cycle count.
effectiveness_verification: Destructive-test sampling over next quarter shows weld quality within spec across all gauge ranges; revised replacement schedule documented and in use.

non_conformance_description: Weld joint failure occurred shortly after a planned welder maintenance event, Line 2, first joint of the shift after restart.
five_why: Why 1: First post-maintenance joint failed -> weld parameters had reverted to factory default settings after the maintenance reset.
Why 2: Reverted to default -> the maintenance procedure required a controller reset that clears custom parameter recipes unless manually backed up first.
Why 3: Not backed up -> the maintenance work instruction does not include a parameter-backup step before performing a controller reset.
Why 4: Backup step missing -> the work instruction was written by the equipment vendor for generic maintenance and was adopted without adding plant-specific pre-work steps.

Why 5 (root cause): the welder maintenance work instruction, adopted directly from the equipment vendor's generic version, was never supplemented with a plant-specific parameter-backup step before controller resets.
root_cause: The welder maintenance work instruction was adopted directly from the equipment vendor's generic version without adding a plant-specific step to back up custom weld parameters before performing a controller reset, so resets silently revert to factory defaults.
corrective_action: Restore the correct weld parameter recipe immediately; inspect and disposition the failed joint and downstream material.
preventive_action: Add a mandatory parameter-backup step to the welder maintenance work instruction before any controller reset, plus a post-maintenance parameter-verification check before resuming production.
effectiveness_verification: Zero post-maintenance parameter-reversion incidents over next 10 maintenance events; verification check documented as completed each time.

non_conformance_description: Low-contrast staining found on finished coil FN-0601 surface, initially misidentified as oil spot during inspection before being confirmed as water spot via lab analysis.
five_why: Why 1: Staining present -> residual moisture was not fully removed during the drying step.
Why 2: Moisture not removed -> drying air temperature was below the validated setpoint for the current line speed.
Why 3: Temperature below setpoint -> the drying unit's heater bank had one element offline, reducing total heat output.
Why 4: Element offline undetected -> the drying unit's control system reports average temperature across all elements, masking a single-element failure as a small overall deviation.

Why 5 (root cause): the drying unit's control system reports an averaged temperature across all heating elements rather than per-element status, so a single failed element is masked as a minor overall deviation instead of being flagged as a fault.
root_cause: The drying unit's control system reports only an averaged temperature across all heater elements, masking a single failed element as a small overall deviation rather than surfacing it as a distinct fault.
corrective_action: Replace the failed heater element immediately; re-dry or disposition affected coils.
preventive_action: Upgrade the drying unit's control system to monitor and report per-element status, with an alarm for any individual element reading outside expected range regardless of the averaged total.
effectiveness_verification: Per-element temperature logs show all elements within range over next 30 days; zero water-spot defects traced to drying insufficiency in that window.

non_conformance_description: Oil spot staining found on coil FN-0615, traced to residual rolling lubricant not fully removed during the cleaning stage prior to finishing.
five_why: Why 1: Residual lubricant present -> cleaning stage effectiveness was reduced for this coil.
Why 2: Reduced effectiveness -> cleaning solution concentration had dropped below the validated range.
